description: First reviewed-core expansion batch. Two existing protocols are promoted only after their public actions are narrowed to the reviewed source; two existing practical templates retain practical status while reviewed Evidence Decisions explicitly reject unsupported specificity.

active-listening-exercises.note: Promoted after aligning the public protocol with a randomized informal-helping-conversation study of trained active listening. The source supports open questions, paraphrasing, reflecting feelings and assumption checking as supportive-listening behaviors associated with greater perceived emotional awareness/supportiveness and emotional improvement in that study. Brali does not claim guaranteed understanding, agreement, relational assurance, problem solving, or conflict resolution.

10-minute-language-microsprints.note: Promoted only after narrowing the effective protocol from a generic ten-minute language session to short L2 vocabulary retrieval practice with later revisits. The reviewed scholarship supports spaced repetition combined with retrieval practice or semantic elaboration as useful vocabulary-training ingredients. Ten minutes is retained only as a convenient optional session label, not an evidence-backed dose, and the claim is not generalized to every language skill.

research_candidates.title: The Role of Active Listening in Informal Helping Conversations: Impact on Perceptions of Listener Helpfulness, Sensitivity, and Supportiveness and Discloser Emotional Improvement
research_candidates.review_notes: Reviewed to support a bounded active-listening protocol. The randomized study supports perceived support/emotional improvement in an informal helping context, not guaranteed problem solving, agreement, relational assurance, or universal conflict resolution.

research_candidates.title: A Review of Laboratory Studies of Adult Second Language Vocabulary Training
research_candidates.review_notes: Reviewed as support for a narrow L2 vocabulary protocol using retrieval and spacing. The review does not establish ten minutes as an optimal dose and does not justify treating one vocabulary-training result as evidence for listening, pronunciation, grammar, or language learning in general.

research_candidates.title: Give me a break! A systematic review and meta-analysis on the efficacy of micro-breaks for increasing well-being and performance
research_candidates.review_notes: Reviewed to bound Pomodoro claims. The meta-analysis supports micro-breaks more clearly for vigor/fatigue than for general task performance and does not establish a 25-minute work/5-minute break schedule as optimal.

research_candidates.title: Building a practically useful theory of goal setting and task motivation: A 35-year odyssey
research_candidates.review_notes: Reviewed to bound the 3×3 workday template. Goal-setting theory supports concrete challenging goals and feedback as useful ingredients under appropriate conditions, but it is not direct evidence for exactly three day blocks, three outcomes per block, nine tasks, or any inherited productivity percentage.

evidence_decisions.source_title: The Role of Active Listening in Informal Helping Conversations: Impact on Perceptions of Listener Helpfulness, Sensitivity, and Supportiveness and Discloser Emotional Improvement
evidence_decisions.citation_text: Bodie GD, Vickery AJ, Cannava K, Jones SM. Western Journal of Communication. 2015;79(2):151-173.
evidence_decisions.study_design: Undergraduate participants were randomly assigned to disclose a recent upsetting problem to a trained active listener or an untrained listener. Trained listeners used open questions, paraphrasing, reflection of feelings, assumption checking and nonverbal immediacy.
evidence_decisions.population: Undergraduate students discussing a recent upsetting problem in an informal helping-conversation study.
evidence_decisions.intervention_or_exposure: Conversation with a trained active listener versus an untrained listener.
evidence_decisions.supported_claim: In this randomized informal helping-conversation study, trained active-listening behaviors were perceived as signaling more emotional awareness/supportiveness and were associated with greater emotional improvement than untrained listening.
unsupported_or_overstated_claims: Active listening guarantees accurate understanding, agreement, trust, or conflict resolution.
Active listening necessarily improves problem-solving utility; this study did not find that effect.
One exact script, number of questions, eye-contact duration, or repetition count is scientifically established.
The study validates active listening equally across workplaces, intimate relationships, therapy, crisis situations, and every culture.
limitations: The sample consisted of undergraduate students in an informal helping-conversation context.
The trained condition bundled several verbal and nonverbal behaviors, so the study does not isolate one universally necessary technique.
Perceived support and emotional improvement are not the same as agreement, durable relationship change, or successful problem solving.
The study does not validate Brali's exact wording or require active listening in every conversation.
evidence_decisions.notes: Use as a bounded supportive-listening protocol: let the speaker finish a thought, paraphrase meaning, invite correction, and ask an open question when useful. Do not promise problem resolution.

evidence_decisions.source_title: A Review of Laboratory Studies of Adult Second Language Vocabulary Training
evidence_decisions.citation_text: Rice CA, Tokowicz N. Studies in Second Language Acquisition. 2020;42(2):439-470.
evidence_decisions.study_design: State-of-the-scholarship review of laboratory studies of adult second-language vocabulary training, organized around how training methods build orthographic, phonological and meaning representations and connections among them.
evidence_decisions.population: Adult second-language learners represented in the laboratory vocabulary-training literature reviewed by the authors.
evidence_decisions.intervention_or_exposure: Vocabulary-training methods including repetition, spacing, retrieval practice and semantic elaboration.
evidence_decisions.supported_claim: The reviewed adult L2 vocabulary literature supports pairing repetition with methods that strengthen form-meaning connections, including spaced repetition with retrieval practice or semantic elaboration requiring learner-generated responses, rather than relying on massed repetition alone.
unsupported_or_overstated_claims: Ten minutes is a scientifically optimal language-learning session length.
A generic micro-sprint improves vocabulary, listening, pronunciation, grammar and speaking equally.
One short session is sufficient for durable vocabulary learning.
Spacing and retrieval have one universal best schedule for every learner, language and word type.
The review supports an inherited percentage improvement or streak target.
limitations: The review focuses on adult second-language vocabulary training, not language learning as a whole.
The reviewed studies vary in training method, material, test and learner characteristics.
The review identifies useful training principles but does not establish a universal session duration or spacing schedule.
Laboratory vocabulary outcomes should not be treated as direct evidence for communicative fluency or every real-world language skill.
evidence_decisions.notes: Narrow the public protocol to a small vocabulary set: retrieve before revealing, check/correct, and revisit on later sessions. Keep ten minutes optional, not evidence-backed.

evidence_decisions.source_title: Give me a break! A systematic review and meta-analysis on the efficacy of micro-breaks for increasing well-being and performance
evidence_decisions.citation_text: Albulescu P, Macsinga I, Rusu A, Sulea C, Bodnaru A, Tulbure BT. PLOS ONE. 2022;17(8):e0272460.
evidence_decisions.study_design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of micro-break studies using breaks of ten minutes or less across work-like and laboratory tasks.
evidence_decisions.population: Participants across the micro-break studies included in the review and meta-analysis.
evidence_decisions.intervention_or_exposure: Short non-work micro-breaks of varying duration and activity.
evidence_decisions.supported_claim: Across the reviewed studies, micro-breaks had clearer average benefits for well-being outcomes such as vigor and fatigue than for overall task performance; performance effects varied by task and break characteristics.
unsupported_or_overstated_claims: Twenty-five minutes of work followed by five minutes of rest is a scientifically optimal schedule.
Pomodoro timing generally improves throughput, accuracy, error rates, or productivity by a fixed percentage.
Every cognitively demanding task benefits from a short break of the same duration.
The meta-analysis validates Brali's 25-minute timer as an evidence-based dose.
limitations: Break activities, durations, tasks and performance measures varied across studies.
The review did not test one standardized Pomodoro 25/5 protocol.
Performance benefits were not uniformly significant and appeared more favorable for less cognitively demanding tasks.
Risk of bias was mixed or unclear across much of the included evidence.
evidence_decisions.notes: Keep the existing Pomodoro entry practical. Its public wording already treats 25 minutes as a starting setting rather than a scientific optimum; this decision records why that boundary must remain.

evidence_decisions.source_title: Building a practically useful theory of goal setting and task motivation: A 35-year odyssey
evidence_decisions.citation_text: Locke EA, Latham GP. American Psychologist. 2002;57(9):705-717.
evidence_decisions.study_design: Integrative review and theory article summarizing approximately 35 years of goal-setting research and its moderators and mechanisms.
evidence_decisions.population: Multiple laboratory and field populations represented in the goal-setting research summarized by the authors.
evidence_decisions.intervention_or_exposure: Goal-setting characteristics and related mechanisms including goal specificity/difficulty and feedback.
evidence_decisions.supported_claim: Goal-setting research summarized by Locke and Latham supports the usefulness of specific, appropriately challenging goals and feedback under relevant conditions; it does not prescribe one universal daily task-count template.
unsupported_or_overstated_claims: Exactly three workday blocks and exactly three outcomes per block are scientifically optimal.
Nine planned tasks per day are an evidence-based productivity target.
A 3×3 structure by itself produces a fixed productivity, completion-rate, context-switching, or time-saving improvement.
Goal-setting theory directly validates the Brali 3×3 workday scaffold.
limitations: This is a broad theory/review article, not a trial of the Brali 3×3 planning format.
Goal effects depend on task characteristics, commitment, ability, feedback and other moderators discussed in the literature.
A daily planning scaffold can be useful without its exact number of blocks or tasks being empirically privileged.
The source does not justify inherited quantitative productivity claims for this protocol.
evidence_decisions.notes: Keep the 3×3 entry practical and explicitly flexible. Use goal-setting research only to support clear outcomes and feedback/review as general ingredients, not the exact numerical scaffold.
